outcome: Guy's conjecture (that the Sprague-Grundy/nim-sequence of every finite octal game is eventually periodic) remains open; no case, counterexample, or bound relevant to this exact (impartial) conjecture was found dated after 26 January 2024.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet is Guy's conjecture for impartial octal games: every finite octal game's nim-sequence is eventually periodic. I checked the two standing reference resources for this problem — Achim Flammenkamp's octal-games database (wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/octal.html, last touched with a July 2026 note that a contributor 'extend[ed] the sgv-sequence of lots of octal-games,' i.e. computed further terms of already-known sequences rather than settling any new game's eventual periodicity) and David Eppstein's 'Octal periodicity' page — plus the current 'Octal game' Wikipedia article, none of which report any octal game's periodicity status changing since January 2024. The one live GitHub artifact the triage found, google-deepmind/formal-conjectures issue #3697 (opened 2026-04-05), is only a request/plan to state Guy's conjecture formally in Lean; it lists the Mathlib building blocks needed and explicitly leaves the proof open — no proof or disproof exists there. The triage's other lead, arXiv:2608.13273 ('A Finite Automaton Approach to Combinatorial Games,' 2026-08), does solve many two-digit games and states results toward a Guy's-conjecture analogue, but its abstract is explicit that this is a *partizan* version of Guy's conjecture ('we propose a partizan version of Guy's conjecture'), a different, non-impartial game class from the one this Wikipedia bullet states; per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated (impartial) conjecture, so it does not count as a change in scope. A tangential lead turned up while searching, arXiv:2512.24221 ('Node-Kayles on Trees,' 2026-01-01), proves periodicity results for Node-Kayles played on trees, but Node-Kayles-on-paths (the linear game, equal to octal game 0.137/Dawson's-Kayles-adjacent) is a different structure from Node-Kayles-on-trees, so this is also a related problem rather than a case of the finite-octal-game conjecture as stated (which concerns heap games on a line, not tree structures). No AI system appears anywhere in this search: the automaton paper uses classical finite-automaton construction and formal verification, not machine learning, and the formal-conjectures GitHub issue is human-authored planning text with no AI-generated content credited. I conclude 'open' with no change found, at high confidence for the impartial conjecture as literally stated, tempered slightly by the fact that the octal-games literature is scattered across personal pages and small journals that a search engine may not fully index.
competing_reading: If a reader takes 'octal games' broadly enough to include the automaton paper's partizan variant or the Node-Kayles-on-trees periodicity results as 'a case of' the conjecture, one could code this as `partial` with an AI role of `none`. I don't think that reading survives contact with the stated question, since both papers change the object (partizan payoff structure; tree adjacency structure) rather than restricting the same impartial, linear-heap game class — but the boundary between 'restriction' and 'variant' in combinatorial game theory is genuinely blurry when a paper explicitly frames its result as an analogue of the named conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or database update that (a) proves or disproves eventual periodicity for a specific unsolved impartial octal game (e.g. one of the ~65 unsettled 2-digit or 8 unsettled 3-digit games listed on Flammenkamp's page, or Grundy's Game / 0.6111...), or (b) exhibits a finite octal game whose nim-sequence is proven non-eventually-periodic, dated after 26 January 2024 — either would move this out of 'open.' Absent that, the conjecture stays open regardless of adjacent partizan or tree-game results.
